verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,
and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper,
then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.
The priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthen vessel over running water.
As for the living bird, he shall take it, and the cedar wood, and the scarlet, and the hyssop, and shall dip them and the living bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the running water.
He shall sprinkle on him who is to be cleansed from the leprosy seven times, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird go into the open field.

“He who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes, and shave off all his hair, and bathe himself in water; and he shall be clean. After that he shall come into the camp, but shall dwell outside his tent seven days.

It shall be on the seventh day, that he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows, even all his hair he shall shave off. He shall wash his clothes, and he shall bathe his body in water, then he shall be clean.

“On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without defect, and one ewe lamb a year old without defect, and three tenths of an ephah  of fine flour for a meal offering, mingled with oil, and one log of oil.
The priest who cleanses him shall set the man who is to be cleansed, and those things, before Yahweh, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
“The priest shall take one of the male lambs, and offer him for a trespass offering, with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before Yahweh.

He shall kill the male lamb in the place where they kill the sin offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary; for as the sin offering is the priest’s, so is the trespass offering. It is most holy.

The priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and the priest shall put it on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.
The priest shall take some of the log of oil, and pour it into the palm of his own left hand.
The priest shall dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand, and shall sprinkle some of the oil with his finger seven times before Yahweh.

The priest shall put some of the rest of the oil that is in his hand on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, upon the blood of the trespass offering.
The rest of the oil that is in the priest’s hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, and the priest shall make atonement for him before Yahweh.
“The priest shall offer the sin offering, and make atonement for him who is to be cleansed because of his uncleanness: and afterward he shall kill the burnt offering;
and the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the meal offering on the altar. The priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean.

“If he is poor, and can’t afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and one tenth of an ephah  of fine flour mingled with oil for a meal offering, and a log of oil;
and two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, such as he is able to afford; and the one shall be a sin offering, and the other a burnt offering.
“On the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the door of the Tent of Meeting, before Yahweh.
The priest shall take the lamb of the trespass offering, and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before Yahweh.

He shall kill the lamb of the trespass offering. The priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering and put it on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.
The priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand;
and the priest shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before Yahweh.

Then the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, on the place of the blood of the trespass offering.
The rest of the oil that is in the priest’s hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before Yahweh.
He shall offer one of the turtledoves, or of the young pigeons, such as he is able to afford,

even such as he is able to afford, the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, with the meal offering. The priest shall make atonement for him who is to be cleansed before Yahweh.”
This is the law for him in whom is the plague of leprosy, who is not able to afford the sacrifice for his cleansing.
Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,
“When you have come into the land of Canaan, which I give to you for a possession, and I put a spreading mildew in a house in the land of your possession,
then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, saying, ‘There seems to me to be some sort of plague in the house.’

The priest shall command that they empty the house, before the priest goes in to examine the plague, that all that is in the house not be made unclean. Afterward the priest shall go in to inspect the house.
He shall examine the plague; and behold, if the plague is in the walls of the house with hollow streaks, greenish or reddish, and it appears to be deeper than the wall;
then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house, and shut up the house seven days.
The priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the plague has spread in the walls of the house,
then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the plague, and cast them into an unclean place outside of the city:
and he shall cause the inside of the house to be scraped all over, and they shall pour out the mortar, that they scraped off, outside of the city into an unclean place.
They shall take other stones, and put them in the place of those stones; and he shall take other mortar, and shall plaster the house.
“If the plague comes again, and breaks out in the house, after he has taken out the stones, and after he has scraped the house, and after it was plastered;
then the priest shall come in and look; and behold, if the plague has spread in the house, it is a destructive mildew in the house. It is unclean.
He shall break down the house, its stones, and its timber, and all the house’s mortar. He shall carry them out of the city into an unclean place.
“Moreover he who goes into the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening.
He who lies down in the house shall wash his clothes; and he who eats in the house shall wash his clothes.

“If the priest shall come in, and examine it, and behold, the plague hasn’t spread in the house, after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, because the plague is healed.
To cleanse the house he shall take two birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.
He shall kill one of the birds in an earthen vessel over running water.
He shall take the cedar wood, and the hyssop, and the scarlet, and the living bird, and dip them in the blood of the slain bird, and in the running water, and sprinkle the house seven times.
He shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird, and with the running water, with the living bird, with the cedar wood, with the hyssop, and with the scarlet;
but he shall let the living bird go out of the city into the open field. So shall he make atonement for the house; and it shall be clean.”
This is the law for any plague of leprosy, and for an itch,
and for the destructive mildew of a garment, and for a house,
and for a rising, and for a scab, and for a bright spot;
to teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean. This is the law of leprosy.

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks about cleansing. Before we hear the law, He speaks it—His voice precedes the remedy. Isn't that how it always is? He speaks, and then the pathway opens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A leper who is healed—notice the text says 'healed' first, before the cleansing ritual. The healing is the Lord's work; the ritual declares it and restores him to the community. How gently the path home is laid out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest goes out of the camp to meet him—not sending word, but going. When Jesus made His lepers clean, He touched them where they waited, far from the gates. The priesthood that moves toward the afflicted bears His character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop—each element speaks. The birds are living and clean; cedar endures; scarlet shouts of blood-price and restoration; hyssop brushes clean. The ritual itself teaches what grace looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One bird is killed over running water. Life poured out, and the waters carry it forward. One dies so the other may be freed—isn't that redemption's pattern?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The living bird is dipped in death and blood, then set free to fly. We are not left abandoned in our guilt—we are bathed in the remedy and sent into the open field. What a comfort this ritual holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sprinklings, then a proclamation: 'You are clean.' The word declares what the blood has already accomplished. His name is called over us, and we are restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wash clothes, shave off all hair, bathe—a complete shedding of what was marked. He comes back into camp, but waits seven more days outside the tent. Healing is one thing; trust rebuilds day by day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day, everything is repeated—all hair off, clothes washed, body bathed. Then he is clean. The sevenfold nature of it reminds us that restoration touches every part of us, and takes time to settle into our bones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the eighth day—a new beginning, the first day of a new week—he brings his offering: two spotless lambs, one ewe lamb, flour, oil. Not one sacrifice, but a full reckoning. His gratitude is written in what he brings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest sets him before the Lord at the door of the Tent of Meeting. He is presented—brought into the holy space, brought before the God who healed him. What a gift, to stand at the threshold again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lamb is offered as a trespass offering, waved with oil before the Lord. His restoration cost something—a life, an oil. He doesn't come cheap into the congregation. The price paid makes the welcome real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lamb is killed in the holy place, as a most holy offering. His cleansing is drawn from the same wellspring as priestly atonement—the Lord takes his healing as seriously as He takes His own holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blood on the right ear, right thumb, right toe—marked for hearing, for work, for walking. His whole body is claimed as clean. The marks of the covenant touch him where he acts and goes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest pours oil into his own palm—a vessel preparing to give. Before anointing him, the priest must hold the oil. We too are vessels, called to carry what the Lord gives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dipping his finger seven times and sprinkling before the Lord—each gesture deliberate, witnessed. The cleansing is not hidden; it is done openly, before the throne of heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The oil—the sign of anointing—touches ear, thumb, toe, upon the blood. He is set apart, holy, fitted for service. This is what restoration looks like: not just accepted back, but anointed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of the oil is poured on his head, and atonement is made. His whole person—from head to the smallest part—is bathed in mercy. 'As the dew falls from the head of Aaron,' runs the psalm. Here is that dew, healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sin offering is next—atonement for his uncleanness. Sin and sickness are bound together here; both are cleansed. The ritual does not separate them, and neither should we forget their common root in a fallen world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The burnt offering ascends; the meal offering is placed on the altar. Every layer of his being is offered back to the Lord—his repentance, his gratitude, his whole self. And then the priest declares: You are clean.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if he is poor—here the Lord's kindness shows itself again. He cannot afford the full offering? The law makes a way. The same cleansing waits for him, same standing, same grace. Poverty does not close the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Turtledoves or young pigeons, 'such as he is able to afford.' The Lord knows his means and meets him there. His offering is not measured by his wealth, but by his honesty. That is what the Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the eighth day, he brings them to the tent—again on that threshold day, the new day, where new things begin. Whether rich or poor, all meet the Lord on the same ground, at the same door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lamb and oil are waved—his sacrifice is lifted to heaven, made visible to the Lord. Even a poor man's offering rises. Even a sparrow's fall is seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The same blood markings—ear, thumb, toe—whether the man is rich or poor. The covenant touches him the same way. His place in the assembly is not diminished by his poverty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest pours oil into his palm—the same gesture, repeated. Even the poor man receives the anointing oil, the mark of the Spirit's favor. The ritual does not rush; it honors each soul the same way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sprinkles of oil, seven times before the Lord. The number speaks: completion, wholeness, holiness. Poor or rich, the sevenfold grace falls the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oil on ear, thumb, toe, upon the blood—the same anointing, the same setting apart. His hand's work, his ear's hearing, his foot's walk—all claimed as clean. Nothing is left unmarked by grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of the oil crowns his head, and atonement is made. The poor man receives the full word: clean. The Lord's justice and mercy meet in every case.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One of his birds is offered as a sin offering, the other as a burnt offering—the same atoning path, just smaller. Small offerings still reach heaven. The Lord counts what is given, not what is withheld.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest makes atonement for him before the Lord, and he is clean. Poverty has not barred him. He stands before the throne as accepted, as whole. What comfort this is for all who lack means.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the law for him who cannot afford the full sacrifice—a law written for the poor. The Lord does not make His mercy costly to those who have little. He bends toward them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks again to Moses and Aaron—now about houses. Plagues are not just in bodies; they seep into the walls of home. Yet even here, the Lord provides a way forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you have come into the land of Canaan—this is spoken to those entering, those beginning. Even in the promised land, mildew and plague come. The Lord does not promise a life free of trouble, but His presence within it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The owner comes and tells the priest, 'There seems to me to be some sort of plague.' He does not know for certain; he brings his concern. That is where faith begins—in the honest naming of what troubles us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Clear the house before the priest examines it—do not let all become unclean. What good wisdom: move what is clean to safety while truth is being searched. Protect the whole while you tend the part.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Greenish or reddish streaks, deeper than the wall—the signs are visible to those who look. Not every spot is plague; judgment requires careful seeing. We too must learn to discern.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The house is shut up for seven days—the Lord's number again. Time is given for the plague to declare itself, for the truth to emerge. Some things cannot be hurried.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day the priest returns to look. Has it spread or stayed? The inquiry is thorough, the judgment is waiting. The Lord gives time, but He does not ignore what festering requires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The infected stones are cast into an unclean place outside the city—they are removed, not hidden. What is corrupt must go out. There is no healing by concealment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inside is scraped all over, the mortar poured out—a thorough cleansing. Every surface is exposed, renewed. This is what turning from sin looks like: not a surface wash, but a deep scraping away of what corrupted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: New stones, new mortar—the house is remade. What was broken is replaced with fresh material. This is restoration's hope: we are not permanently scarred by what we remove.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the plague comes again—not 'if,' but more accurately 'when we discover it has come again'—even after all is scrubbed and replaced. Sometimes the roots run deeper than we first see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then the house is declared destructive, unclean. Some things cannot be healed by repair. Sometimes letting go is the only path forward. The Lord does not ask us to live in corruption for sentiment's sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole house is torn down and carried to an unclean place—stones, timber, mortar. A radical end. Yet there is mercy even here: the owner is not destroyed; only what cannot be redeemed is taken away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who enters the shut-up house becomes unclean. We are marked by what we touch, what we dwell in. Be careful what you expose yourself to; it enters you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who lie down or eat there must wash their clothes—even ordinary acts in an unclean place require cleansing. Small exposures, small contaminations, yet they matter. The Lord minds the details.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the priest comes and sees the plague has not spread—then the house is clean. The same house, the same walls, yet now pronounced whole. Healing comes when the corruption is truly gone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop—the same elements that cleansed the leper now cleanse the house. The tools of healing are the same; they speak the same language of atonement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One bird is killed over running water. Again the pattern: one dies so others live. The price is paid in blood. Home, like bodies, is redeemed at a cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cedar, hyssop, scarlet, and the living bird are dipped in blood and running water, then the house is sprinkled seven times. Every corner is touched. The cleansing is thorough and witnessed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The house is cleansed with blood and water, with the living bird and the fragrant wood, with scarlet and hyssop—a symphony of symbols, all pointing to how deep the cleansing goes. No single gesture suffices; the whole ritual is the word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The living bird is sent out to the open field—freedom for what carries the cleansing. And so atonement is made for the house; it becomes clean again. The Lord restores what was marked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the law for plague, for itch—all forms of corruption are met by the same framework of inspection and cleansing. The Lord's mercy covers more than we imagine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For garments, for houses—corruption spreads; it infects. Yet each corruption is named, each has a path to cleansing. The Lord does not leave us to guess or to despair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rising, scab, bright spot—the various marks of corruption. Each is seen, each is counted. The Lord's eye misses nothing that troubles us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean—readers today hear an echo here: we live in a time of great confusion about what marks us as unclean before God. Yet the lesson remains: the Lord Himself declares us clean through the blood of Christ, and that word stands. We need not wander in shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
